title: Multivariable Calculus
description: Partial derivatives, the gradient, Jacobians and the chain rule, the Hessian, matrix calculus identities and multiple integrals.
overview: A machine learning model has thousands or billions of parameters, so its loss is a function of many variables. To minimize it we need the multivariable versions of the derivative. The gradient collects all the partial derivatives and points uphill. The Jacobian describes how a vector-valued function changes, and its chain rule is backpropagation. The Hessian measures curvature and decides whether a critical point is a minimum.

This chapter builds these objects, derives the matrix-calculus identities that appear in least squares, logistic regression and neural networks, and ends with multiple integrals and the change-of-variables formula that normalizes the Gaussian.
objectives: Compute partial derivatives and the gradient, and use the gradient to find the direction of steepest ascent and a directional derivative.
Compute a Jacobian and apply the multivariable chain rule.
Compute the Hessian, write the second-order Taylor approximation and classify critical points.
Use the standard matrix-calculus identities for linear and quadratic forms.
Evaluate double integrals, use polar coordinates, and state the change-of-variables formula.

sections.title: Partial derivatives and the gradient
body: For a function f(x₁, …, x_n) of several variables, the **partial derivative** ∂f/∂x_i is the ordinary derivative with respect to x_i, treating all the other variables as constants. The **gradient** collects them into a vector:

example.title: A gradient
example.problem: Find the gradient of f(x, y) = x² + xy + 2y² and evaluate it at (1, 1).
example.solution: ∂f/∂x = 2x + y and ∂f/∂y = x + 4y, so ∇f = (2x + y, x + 4y). At (1, 1) the gradient is (3, 5).

body: The **directional derivative** of f at x in the direction of a unit vector u is the rate of change along that direction, and it equals a dot product:

where θ is the angle between ∇f and u. The right side is largest when θ = 0, so the gradient points in the direction of **steepest ascent**, and its length is the steepest rate of increase. The direction −∇f is the steepest descent, which is the reason gradient descent moves against the gradient. The gradient is also perpendicular to the **level sets** (contours) {x : f(x) = c}, because moving along a contour does not change f.

example.title: A directional derivative
example.problem: For f(x, y) = x² + xy + 2y² at (1, 1), find D_u f for u = (1, 0) and for the steepest-descent direction.
example.solution: D_u f = (3, 5)·(1, 0) = 3. The steepest descent direction is −(3, 5)/√34, along which the rate of change is −‖(3, 5)‖ = −√34 = −5.83. Moving a small distance ε in that direction reduces f by about 5.83ε.

body.warn: For elongated contours the negative gradient points across the valley, not at the minimum. This is why plain gradient descent zigzags on badly scaled problems.

sections.title: Jacobians and the chain rule
body: For a function f : ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ with components f₁, …, f_m, the **Jacobian matrix** is the m × n matrix of all partial derivatives, J_ij = ∂f_i/∂x_j. It is the best linear approximation to f near a point: f(x + d) ≈ f(x) + J d. For m = 1 the Jacobian is the transpose of the gradient.

example.title: A Jacobian
example.problem: Find the Jacobian of f(x, y) = (x²y, 5x + sin y) and evaluate it at (1, π).

body: The **chain rule** for compositions says that Jacobians multiply: if h = g ∘ f, then J_h(x) = J_g(f(x)) · J_f(x). For a scalar loss L at the end of a chain x → z → a → L, the gradient is a product of Jacobians, evaluated from the output backward:

Backpropagation computes this right-to-left, so that each step multiplies a Jacobian transpose by a //vector// (the gradient flowing back), a **vector–Jacobian product**. It never forms the full Jacobians, whose size would be enormous. This ordering is why reverse mode is efficient for a scalar loss with many inputs.

example.title: One layer of a network
example.problem: For a layer z = Wx + b, a = σ(z) (elementwise) and loss L, write ∂L/∂z, ∂L/∂W and ∂L/∂x in terms of the upstream gradient g = ∂L/∂a.
solution: The Jacobian of the elementwise σ is diagonal, with entries σ′(z_i), so ∂L/∂z = g ⊙ σ′(z) =: δ.
For z = Wx + b: ∂L/∂W = δ xᵀ, ∂L/∂b = δ and ∂L/∂x = Wᵀδ. These are exactly the backpropagation equations of the Machine Learning book.

body: For p = softmax(z), ∂p_i/∂z_j = p_i(δ_ij − p_j) (with δ_ij the Kronecker delta), so J = diag(p) − ppᵀ. Every row sums to zero, because the probabilities sum to one and any increase in one must be matched by decreases in the others.

sections.title: The Hessian and second-order approximation
body: The **Hessian** of a scalar function is the symmetric matrix of second partial derivatives, H_ij = ∂²f/∂x_i∂x_j. (Mixed partials are equal when they are continuous.) It describes curvature in every direction: the second derivative along a unit direction u is uᵀHu.
The second-order Taylor approximation near x is

body.eq: f(x + d) ≈ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ d + ½ dᵀ H(x) d

body: At a critical point (∇f = 0) the behavior is governed by H:

list: H positive definite (all eigenvalues > 0): a local **minimum**.
H negative definite (all eigenvalues < 0): a local maximum.
H has eigenvalues of both signs: a **saddle point**, which is a minimum in some directions and a maximum in others.
A function is **convex** exactly when H is positive semidefinite everywhere. For a convex function every critical point is a global minimum.

example.title: Classifying critical points
example.problem: Classify the critical points of f(x, y) = x² + xy + 2y² and of g(x, y) = x² − y².
solution: For f, ∇f = (2x + y, x + 4y) = 0 only at the origin. H = [[2, 1], [1, 4]] has trace 6 and determinant 7, so eigenvalues (6 ± √8)/2 = 4.414 and 1.586, both positive. The origin is a minimum, and f is convex.
For g, ∇g = (2x, −2y) = 0 at the origin, with H = diag(2, −2): eigenvalues of both signs. It is a saddle point.

body: Newton's method uses the second-order model: minimizing it over d gives the step d = −H⁻¹∇f, which is a gradient step rescaled by the inverse curvature. In high-dimensional non-convex problems such as neural networks, most critical points are saddles, not local minima, and the Hessian's eigenvalues (the curvature in each direction) determine the largest stable learning rate, 2/λ_max.

example.title: Hessians of two losses
example.problem: Find the Hessian of the least squares loss L(θ) = ‖Xθ − y‖², and say whether it is convex.
example.solution: The gradient is 2Xᵀ(Xθ − y) and the Hessian is 2XᵀX. For any vector v, vᵀXᵀXv = ‖Xv‖² ≥ 0, so the Hessian is positive semidefinite: L is convex, and every critical point (every solution of the normal equations) is a global minimum.

sections.title: Matrix calculus
body: Most machine learning objectives are written with vectors and matrices. A few identities, which can all be checked by writing out the components, handle nearly every case. Here a and b are constant vectors, A is a constant matrix and x is the variable, with the gradient written as a column vector.

example.title: Deriving the normal equations
example.problem: Minimize J(θ) = ‖Xθ − y‖² using the table.
example.solution: ∇J = 2Xᵀ(Xθ − y). Setting it to zero gives XᵀXθ = Xᵀy, the normal equations, and the Hessian 2XᵀX is positive semidefinite, so the solution is a global minimum.

example.title: A check by components
example.solution: xᵀAx = x₁² + 2x₁x₂ + 3x₂². The gradient is (2x₁ + 2x₂, 2x₁ + 6x₂). And (A + Aᵀ)x = [[2, 2], [2, 6]]x = (2x₁ + 2x₂, 2x₁ + 6x₂) ✓.

body: For a scalar function of a matrix X, the gradient ∇_X f has the same shape as X, with entries ∂f/∂X_ij. Useful identities include ∇_X tr(AX) = Aᵀ, ∇_X tr(XᵀAX) = (A + Aᵀ)X, ∇_X ln det X = X⁻ᵀ, and ∇_X ‖X‖_F² = 2X. The trace is handy because tr(AB) = tr(BA) and a scalar equals its own trace: for example aᵀXb = tr(aᵀXb) = tr(baᵀX), so ∇_X aᵀXb = abᵀ.

body.note: Conventions differ. Some books define the derivative of a scalar with respect to a column vector as a row vector (the 'numerator layout'). This book uses the gradient as a column vector throughout, which matches the update θ ← θ − α∇J.

sections.title: Multiple integrals and change of variables
body: A **double integral** ∬ f(x, y) dA gives the volume under a surface. Over a rectangle it is computed as an **iterated integral**, integrating one variable at a time (**Fubini's theorem**, valid for continuous or non-negative f):

body.eq: ∬_{[a,b]×[c,d]} f(x, y) dA = ∫_a^b ( ∫_c^d f(x, y) dy ) dx

example.title: Area of a disc by polar coordinates
example.problem: Find the area of the disc x² + y² ≤ R².
example.solution: ∫₀^{2π} ∫₀^R r dr dθ = 2π · R²/2 = πR². The factor r from the Jacobian is essential: without it the answer would be 2πR.

example.title: A scaling map
example.problem: The map x = Au + b with A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] takes the unit square to a rectangle. What is the area scale factor?
example.solution: |det A| = 6. The unit square has area 1 and the image rectangle (2 by 3) has area 6.

summary: The gradient ∇f collects partial derivatives; it points in the direction of steepest ascent, is perpendicular to level sets, and gives D_u f = ∇fᵀu.
The Jacobian of f : ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ is an m × n matrix; the chain rule multiplies Jacobians. Backpropagation evaluates vector–Jacobian products from the output backward.

The Hessian gives the second-order Taylor model f(x + d) ≈ f + ∇fᵀd + ½dᵀHd. Positive definite Hessian at a critical point means a minimum, mixed signs mean a saddle, and positive semidefinite everywhere means convex.
Key identities: ∇aᵀx = a, ∇xᵀAx = (A + Aᵀ)x, ∇‖Ax − b‖² = 2Aᵀ(Ax − b); they give the normal equations.
Double integrals are iterated integrals (Fubini). Under a change of variables, volumes scale by |det J|. In polar coordinates dx dy = r dr dθ, which proves ∫e^{−x²/2}dx = √(2π).

problems.q: Find the gradient and the Hessian of f(x, y, z) = x²y + yz² and evaluate the gradient at (1, 2, 3).
Find the minimum of f(x, y) = x² + 2y² − 2x + 4y.
problems.solution: ∇f = (2x − 2, 4y + 4) = 0 gives (1, −1). H = diag(2, 4) is positive definite, so this is the global minimum, with f = 1 + 2 − 2 − 4 = −3.

problems.q: Compute the Jacobian of f(x, y) = (e^x cos y, e^x sin y) and its determinant.
problems.solution: J = [[e^x cos y, −e^x sin y], [e^x sin y, e^x cos y]], with determinant e^{2x}(cos²y + sin²y) = e^{2x}.

problems.q: For f(θ) = ½θᵀAθ − bᵀθ with A = [[2, 0], [0, 4]] and b = (2, 4), find the minimizer, and the largest stable gradient descent step size.
problems.solution: ∇f = Aθ − b = 0 gives θ = A⁻¹b = (1, 1). The Hessian is A with eigenvalues 2 and 4, so gradient descent is stable for α < 2/4 = 0.5.

problems.q: Compute ∬ over the unit square of x y² dA.
problems.solution: The integrand factorizes: ∫₀¹ x dx · ∫₀¹ y² dy = (1/2)(1/3) = 1/6.
